questions.stem: A patient has pinpoint pupils, slow shallow breathing, and is barely rousable. Which toxidrome is this?
questions.why: Miosis, respiratory depression and a depressed level of consciousness is the opioid triad. The respiratory rate is what kills, and it is what naloxone is aimed at — not waking the patient up.

options.t: Opioid
Sympathomimetic
options.why: Stimulants dilate pupils and speed everything up.

options.t: Cholinergic
options.why: Cholinergics constrict pupils but flood the patient with secretions.

options.t: Anticholinergic
options.why: Anticholinergics dilate pupils and leave the skin hot and dry.

questions.stem: Hot, dry, flushed skin with dilated pupils, retention and delirium describes which toxidrome?
questions.why: Mad as a hatter, red as a beet, dry as a bone, blind as a bat, hot as a hare. Antihistamines, tricyclics, jimson weed and several antipsychotics all produce it — the dryness is what separates it from cholinergic.

options.t: Cholinergic
options.why: Cholinergic patients are wet, not dry — that is the whole distinction.

options.t: Sedative-hypnotic
options.why: Sedatives depress consciousness without the hot dry skin or dilated pupils.

options.t: Opioid
options.why: Opioids constrict pupils and depress breathing.

options.t: Anticholinergic

questions.stem: What does SLUDGE describe, and which exposure produces it?
questions.why: Salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, emesis — every secretion at once. Add bradycardia, bronchorrhea and bronchospasm and the patient drowns in their own fluids. Atropine dries them; that is the point of very large doses.

options.t: Withdrawal from long-term alcohol use
options.why: Withdrawal produces tremor, agitation and autonomic instability without the secretions.

options.t: Serotonin syndrome from combined antidepressants
options.why: Serotonin syndrome features clonus, rigidity and hyperthermia.

options.t: Cholinergic excess — organophosphates
Anticholinergic effects from antihistamine overdose
options.why: Antihistamines dry the patient out, the opposite of SLUDGE.

questions.stem: Per the program's drug sheet, what is the adult atropine dose for organophosphate poisoning?
questions.why: The sheet gives 2 to 4 mg repeated every three to five minutes until blood pressure and heart rate stabilize. Unlike bradycardia, there is no 3 mg ceiling here — the endpoint is drying the secretions, and it can take a great deal.

options.t: 0.02 mg/kg IV/IO to a maximum of 0.5 mg
options.why: That is the pediatric bradycardia dose.

options.t: 1 mg IV/IO every 3 to 5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg
options.why: That is the unstable bradycardia dose, far too little here.

options.t: 0.5 mg IV/IO once, then reassess
options.why: A single small dose does not touch a cholinergic crisis.

options.t: 2 to 4 mg IV/IO, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes

questions.stem: What is the clinical endpoint for atropine in an organophosphate exposure?
questions.why: The patient dies from bronchorrhea and bronchospasm, not from the bradycardia. Atropine is titrated until the chest is dry and ventilation is possible, however much that takes.

options.t: A heart rate above 100
options.why: Heart rate is watched, but it is not the endpoint being titrated to.

options.t: Drying of the pulmonary secretions
Pupils returning to a normal size
options.why: Pupil size lags well behind and is not the target.

options.t: Reaching the standard 3 mg total dose
options.why: The cholinergic dose has no such ceiling.

questions.stem: What is the goal when giving naloxone to an opioid overdose?
questions.why: Titrate to respiration. Slamming a full dose into a dependent patient produces violent withdrawal, vomiting into an unprotected airway, and someone who leaves before the naloxone wears off — which it will, before the opioid does.

options.t: Fully reverse the opioid and wake the patient
options.why: Complete reversal risks precipitated withdrawal and a combative patient.

options.t: Confirm that opioids were the cause of the overdose
options.why: A response is suggestive but naloxone is not a diagnostic test.

options.t: Prevent the patient from using opioids again
options.why: Naloxone has no lasting effect on future use.

options.t: Restore adequate breathing, not full consciousness

questions.stem: Why must an opioid overdose reversed by naloxone still be transported?
questions.why: Naloxone lasts roughly 30 to 90 minutes. Fentanyl analogues and long-acting oral opioids outlast it easily, so a patient who refuses transport can go back into respiratory arrest with no one there.

options.t: Naloxone causes delayed cardiac dysrhythmias
options.why: That is not a recognized effect.

options.t: A urine drug screen is legally required
options.why: There is no such requirement driving transport.

options.t: Naloxone wears off before most opioids do
The patient will develop withdrawal seizures
options.why: Opioid withdrawal is miserable but not typically seizure-producing.

questions.stem: Which finding in alcohol withdrawal signals the most dangerous stage?
questions.why: Delirium tremens — confusion, hallucinations, fever, tachycardia and hypertension, typically 48 to 96 hours in — carries real mortality. Alcohol withdrawal is one of the few withdrawals that kills; opioid withdrawal generally does not.

options.t: Nausea and vomiting on the morning after
options.why: Common and not a marker of severity.

options.t: Delirium with autonomic instability
Anxiety with difficulty sleeping
options.why: Early and expected in withdrawal.

options.t: Tremor of the hands starting 8 hours after the last drink
options.why: Early tremor is expected and comparatively benign.

questions.stem: Why should you be cautious attributing altered mental status to intoxication in a known drinker?
questions.why: Chronic drinkers fall, bleed slowly into a subdural, and run low sugars from depleted glycogen. "Just drunk" is a diagnosis of exclusion, and the exclusions are the things that kill.

options.t: Intoxicated patients cannot legally be assessed
options.why: Intoxication affects capacity to refuse, not your ability to assess.

options.t: Blood alcohol cannot be measured in the field
options.why: True, but that is not the reason for caution.

options.t: Alcohol does not actually alter mental status
options.why: Alcohol very much alters mental status.

options.t: Head injury and low sugar are common in them

questions.stem: Which complication most threatens a patient in severe sympathomimetic toxicity?
questions.why: Agitation and muscle activity generate heat the patient cannot shed. Core temperature climbs, muscle breaks down, potassium and myoglobin flood out, and the kidneys and the heart follow. Cooling and sedation are the priorities.

options.t: Profound bradycardia
options.why: Stimulants drive the rate up.

options.t: Respiratory depression
options.why: Stimulants speed respiration rather than depressing it.

options.t: Hyperthermia with rhabdomyolysis
Miosis with a decreased level of consciousness
options.why: That combination belongs to opioids.

questions.stem: Why is excited delirium considered a medical emergency rather than a behavioral one?
questions.why: Extreme agitation, hyperthermia, and a profound metabolic acidosis from sustained muscle activity. Prolonged struggle against restraint accelerates all three — sedation, cooling and monitoring beat holding someone down.

options.t: Restraint is legally prohibited in these cases
options.why: Restraint may be needed; it is how and for how long that matters.

options.t: The condition resolves on its own without treatment
options.why: It carries a real mortality rate.

options.t: These patients arrest from hyperthermia and acidosis
They are more likely to injure responders than other patients
options.why: Safety matters, but that is not what makes it medical.

questions.stem: Which ECG finding signals serious tricyclic antidepressant toxicity?
questions.why: Tricyclics block sodium channels, so the QRS widens and a terminal R wave appears in aVR. A QRS beyond 100 ms predicts seizures and beyond 160 ms predicts dysrhythmias — sodium bicarbonate is the antidote to that blockade.

options.t: A widening QRS with a terminal R in aVR
Peaked T waves across the precordial leads
options.why: That pattern points to hyperkalemia.

options.t: Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression
options.why: That describes pericarditis.

options.t: A shortening QT interval
options.why: Tricyclics prolong the QT rather than shortening it.

questions.stem: Why is acetaminophen overdose particularly dangerous in the first 24 hours?
questions.why: Early acetaminophen toxicity is nausea and malaise at worst, so the patient and often the clinician relax. Meanwhile the liver is being destroyed, and by the time jaundice and coagulopathy appear the window for N-acetylcysteine has narrowed.

options.t: It causes immediate cardiac dysrhythmias
options.why: Acetaminophen is not primarily cardiotoxic.

options.t: It produces severe respiratory depression early
options.why: Respiratory depression is not its pattern.

options.t: The patient often looks and feels well
It causes rapid onset seizures
options.why: Seizures are not a typical early feature.

questions.stem: Why is standard pulse oximetry unreliable in carbon monoxide poisoning?
questions.why: The sensor sees both bound states as saturated, so a poisoned patient reads 99% while carrying almost no oxygen. A CO-oximeter is what distinguishes them — a normal SpO2 rules out nothing.

options.t: The probe fails at the temperatures these patients present with
options.why: Temperature is not the source of the error.

options.t: Carbon monoxide constricts the peripheral vessels
options.why: Peripheral vasoconstriction affects the signal, not the fundamental error.

options.t: Carbon monoxide destroys hemoglobin entirely
options.why: Hemoglobin is bound, not destroyed.

options.t: It cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin

questions.stem: Several people in one household have headache, nausea, and fatigue that improve outdoors. What should you suspect?
questions.why: Multiple people in one building, symptoms worse indoors and better outside, and pets affected too — that pattern is carbon monoxide until proven otherwise. It is also a scene-safety problem before it is a patient problem.

options.t: Natural gas leak causing hypoxia
options.why: Possible, but the flu-like pattern that lifts outdoors is the CO signature.

options.t: Food poisoning from a shared meal
options.why: Food poisoning would not improve simply by stepping outside.

options.t: A viral illness passing through the family
options.why: A virus does not resolve on leaving the building.

options.t: Carbon monoxide exposure

questions.stem: A beta blocker overdose is bradycardic and hypotensive and has not responded to atropine. Per the drug sheet, what comes next?
questions.why: The drug sheet lists beta blocker and calcium channel blocker overdose among the indications for both atropine and push-dose epinephrine. Once the receptor is blocked, you push harder on it — glucagon and calcium are the hospital's next moves.

options.t: Naloxone, since beta blockers act on opioid receptors
options.why: Beta blockers have no opioid receptor activity.

options.t: Amiodarone to stabilize the rhythm
options.why: An antidysrhythmic would worsen a bradycardic, hypotensive patient.

options.t: Push-dose epinephrine, 5 to 20 mcg of 1:100,000
A second and third dose of atropine beyond 3 mg
options.why: Atropine has a 3 mg ceiling and is not the answer once it has failed.

questions.stem: What is the first priority at a scene where a patient has been exposed to a chemical?
questions.why: A contaminated patient is a contamination source. Responders who skip that step become patients themselves, and a contaminated ambulance is out of service. Decontamination happens before treatment beyond the immediate life threats.

options.t: Rapid patient extrication to the ambulance
options.why: Moving a contaminated patient into your ambulance contaminates it and you.

options.t: Identifying the exact chemical involved
options.why: Identification matters but comes after scene safety is established.

options.t: Establishing IV access for antidote administration
options.why: Access on a contaminated patient exposes you directly.

options.t: Your own safety and scene control

questions.stem: What makes pupil size such a useful finding in a poisoned patient?
questions.why: Constricted points toward opioids and cholinergics; dilated toward stimulants, anticholinergics and withdrawal. Combined with the skin — wet or dry — and the vital signs, it gets you to a toxidrome without a name for the drug.

options.t: It splits the toxidromes into two groups
It predicts how long the effects will last
options.why: Duration depends on the agent's pharmacokinetics.

options.t: It correlates directly with the dose taken
options.why: Pupil size does not scale with dose.

options.t: It identifies the specific drug involved
options.why: It narrows the class rather than naming the agent.

questions.stem: Match each toxidrome to its characteristic set of findings.
questions.why: Pupils and skin do most of the sorting. Wet versus dry separates cholinergic from anticholinergic; pupil size separates opioid from stimulant. The specific drug matters far less in the field than the class it belongs to.
pairs: Dilated pupils, fast and hot, agitated and sweaty
Dilated pupils, hot and dry, delirious, retaining urine
Sedation with normal pupils and stable vitals
Ringing ears, fast breathing, fever, vomiting

questions.stem: A patient took an unknown quantity of an unknown pill an hour ago and looks well. What should drive your management?
questions.why: Plenty of agents — acetaminophen, sustained-release preparations, tricyclics — look benign for hours and then are not. Bring the bottle, note the time and quantity, and reassess on the way rather than concluding from a well-looking hour one.

options.t: Supportive care, transport, serial reassessment
Withholding transport until symptoms actually appear
options.why: Many agents have a delay before they become dangerous.

options.t: Giving activated charcoal to every such patient
options.why: Charcoal has narrow indications and real aspiration risk.

options.t: Inducing vomiting to remove the remaining pills
options.why: Induced emesis is not used in prehospital care.

questions.stem: Which finding best distinguishes serotonin syndrome from other hyperthermic toxidromes?
questions.why: Neuromuscular hyperactivity — clonus, hyperreflexia, rigidity worse in the legs — alongside agitation, fever and autonomic instability. It usually follows adding a second serotonergic drug, and the history is often the biggest clue.

options.t: Dry, flushed skin
options.why: Dry flushed skin points to an anticholinergic picture.

options.t: Pinpoint pupils
options.why: Serotonin syndrome dilates pupils rather than constricting them.

options.t: Bradycardia with heavy secretions
options.why: That is the cholinergic pattern.

options.t: Clonus, worst in the lower limbs

questions.stem: Why does the timing of an ingestion matter as much as the substance?
questions.why: A patient one hour into a large acetaminophen ingestion looks fine and is in serious trouble; one six hours into a benzodiazepine is past their peak. The same appearance means opposite things depending on where the clock sits.

options.t: Antidotes expire a fixed time after ingestion
options.why: Antidote windows exist, but the general point is the trajectory.

options.t: It determines which hospital can accept the patient
options.why: Destination depends on capability, not on the clock.

options.t: It establishes whether the ingestion was intentional
options.why: Intent comes from the history and the scene, not the timing.

options.t: It tells you where on the curve the patient is
